newsitem.title: USA: GM faces midnight strike deadline at Cadillac plant.
newsitem.headline: GM faces midnight strike deadline at Cadillac plant.

text.p: General Motors Corp., already battered by seven strikes this year, plans marathon talks with the United Auto Workers Friday ahead of a strike deadline at a key Cadillac luxury car plant in Michigan.

A strike at GM's assembly plant in the Hamtramck, Mich., enclave in Detroit could disrupt the production and marketing launch of the redesigned Seville sedan, which is central to GM's plans to revamp Cadillac's stuffy, land-yacht image.
GM plans to introduce the Seville at next month's auto show in Frankfurt, Germany as a bonafide world-class competitor to Mercedes-Benz AG, BMW AG and Toyota Motor Corp.'s Lexus.
A prolonged strike could delay those plans, as an April walkout in Oklahoma City did with the introduction of GM's mid-size Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass sedans.

The issues that may prompt a strike by 3,600 workers at the Hamtramck plant are similar to those that have spawned seven strikes this year -- demands for more staff to replace retiring workers and curbs on GM's ability to shift work to outside contractors.

Record numbers of workers have been retiring at many GM plants across the country, increasing the burden on remaining employees. The world's largest automaker has shed about 17,000 workers in the past year through retirements and plant sales, and the UAW has demanded replacements.
"When they eliminate these jobs, the other workers have too much work, and it wears them down," said Donald Steele, vice president of UAW Local 22 at the Cadillac plant.
The disputes have been most pronounced at GM plants that are introducing new products, because the automaker has designed them to be built with fewer workers.
Steele added, however, that the union still hoped to reach an agreement before Friday's midnight deadline.

GM spokesman Paul Spadafora said GM also hoped to avert a strike, but added that the talks probably would continue right up to the deadline. He declined to comment on the timing for the Seville launch.

In addition to the Seville, the Hamtramck plant builds the Cadillac DeVille sedan and Eldorado coupe. It also can produce the Buick Park Avenue, which uses the same platform as the Seville, Spadafora said.
The strikes have been costly to GM, cutting second-quarter profits by $490 million and reducing its share of the domestic car and light truck market well below GM's 1997 goal of 33 percent.

The automaker also said Friday that a three-month walkout at a Pontiac, Mich., truck plant and a six-day strike at a Warren, Mich., transmission plant, forced it to cut its third-quarter production schedule by 20,000 vehicles.
The strikes also have hurt GM's efforts to revamp its image among consumers.

Analysts said a seven-week strike at Oklahoma City killed the momentum of GM's advertising launch for the Malibu and Cutlass sedans, two important mid-size sedans designed to undercut Toyota's Camry, Honda Motor Co. Ltd.'s Accord and Ford Motor Co.'s Taurus in price.

"The most damaging thing about the strike in Oklahoma City was that it forced the company to relaunch the Malibu," said Schroder Wertheim & Co. auto analyst John Casesa. "If the strike had not happened, that car would have better awareness and better sales."
GM sold a respectable 12,996 Malibus in July, but that still fell short of the Corsicas and Berettas it replaced, which had sales of 15,698 units for the month.
Analysts also worry that consumers' attention will be drawn away from the car by Honda's launch of an all-new Accord this fall.
